entities.summary:
Darius III (b. 379 BCE, Persis) was a prominent king of the Achaemenid Empire, known for his struggles against Alexander the Great. He was the son of Artaxerxes II and Roxana, and succeeded his brother Artaxerxes IV to the throne. Darius III's reign was marked by a series of military defeats against Alexander's forces, which ultimately led to the conquest of Persia. Despite his failure, Darius III is remembered for his diplomatic efforts to maintain Persian independence and his role in shaping the Achaemenid Empire's cultural heritage.


Darius III's reign was also notable for his economic policies, which aimed to strengthen the empire's finances and infrastructure. He implemented various trade agreements and expanded the empire's borders through a series of military campaigns.


The legacy of Darius III can be seen in the many archaeological sites and artifacts left behind by the Achaemenid Empire, including the famous Persepolis complex. His reign marked the beginning of the end of the Achaemenid Empire, but his impact on Persian history and culture continues to be felt today.


The 329 BCE Battle of Issus, in which Darius III was defeated by Alexander, was a pivotal moment in world history, marking the beginning of the Hellenistic period and the spread of Greek culture throughout the ancient world.


In a famous quote from the Greek historian Arrian, Darius III was described as 'a man of noble birth and a king of great courage', but ultimately 'a king who had been defeated by the gods'.
